title: Synchronous Writes in Distributed System for Strong Consistency

blocks.html: A write operation is considered successful only after all required replicas have confirmed the write.
blocks.text: A write operation is considered successful only after all required replicas have confirmed the write.

blocks.html: Use case: Systems needing strong consistency (e.g., banking, inventory management).

blocks.html: How Synchronous Writes Happen
Client sends the request.
The coordinator sends the request to every replica and waits for the acknowledgement.

blocks.html: Each of the replicas write the data but do not commit.
blocks.text: Each of the replicas write the data but do not commit.

blocks.html: Those who successfully write the data send the acknowledgement of success.
blocks.text: Those who successfully write the data send the acknowledgement of success.

blocks.html: Those who cannot write, first they try again and again for a fixed number of times, even after that if they fail, they send the acknowledgement of failure.

What if?
Replica Acknowledgment Fails
Problem:
A replica successfully writes the data but fails to send an acknowledgment to the coordinator.
blocks.text: A replica successfully writes the data but fails to send an acknowledgment to the coordinator.

blocks.html: The coordinator thinks the replica failed.
blocks.text: The coordinator thinks the replica failed.

blocks.html: Too many sub-problems:
The coordinator may try again and again.
blocks.text: The coordinator may try again and again.

blocks.html: The coordinator may report failure for write which has happened.
blocks.text: The coordinator may report failure for write which has happened.

blocks.html: Solution:
Idempotent writes / unique transaction IDs
Each write has a unique identifier.
blocks.text: Each write has a unique identifier.

blocks.html: Retrying a write on the same replica does not create duplicates.
blocks.text: Retrying a write on the same replica does not create duplicates.

blocks.html: Using the ID, the replica understands that the acknowledgement was not received, so the acknowledgement is sent again.
blocks.text: Using the ID, the replica understands that the acknowledgement was not received, so the acknowledgement is sent again.

blocks.html: Even Resent Acknowledgement Fails
Problem:
The resent acknowledgement fails.
This repeats potentially forever.
Solution:
After N retries or timeout period, coordinator stops retrying and reports failure to the client.
blocks.text: After N retries or timeout period, coordinator stops retrying and reports failure to the client.

blocks.html: System may mark the transaction as “in-doubt” or “pending acknowledgment”.
blocks.text: System may mark the transaction as “in-doubt” or “pending acknowledgment”.

blocks.html: Background processes check for unacknowledged writes and reconcile with coordinator later.

blocks.html: 3. Problems / Challenges in Synchronous Writes
Increased latency:
The write is delayed by the slowest replica in the group.
blocks.text: The write is delayed by the slowest replica in the group.

blocks.html: Availability issues:
If one replica is down or unreachable, the write may fail.
blocks.text: If one replica is down or unreachable, the write may fail.

blocks.html: This reduces system availability (CAP tradeoff: strong consistency vs availability).
blocks.text: This reduces system availability (CAP tradeoff: strong consistency vs availability).

blocks.html: Network partitions / failures:
In case of network split, some nodes may not receive the write, leading to potential write failures.
blocks.text: In case of network split, some nodes may not receive the write, leading to potential write failures.

blocks.html: Write amplification:
Writing to multiple replicas simultaneously increases I/O operations.
blocks.text: Writing to multiple replicas simultaneously increases I/O operations.

blocks.html: Blocking writes under load:
High load on replicas can make synchronous writes slow and block clients.
blocks.text: High load on replicas can make synchronous writes slow and block clients.

blocks.html: 4. Solutions / Techniques to Handle Problems
Quorum-based writes (e.g., W/N+1)
Instead of all replicas, require acknowledgment from a majority (quorum).
blocks.text: Instead of all replicas, require acknowledgment from a majority (quorum).

blocks.html: Reduces latency and allows some failures while maintaining consistency.
blocks.text: Reduces latency and allows some failures while maintaining consistency.

blocks.html: Timeouts and retries
If replicas do not respond within a timeout, coordinator retries or fails gracefully.
blocks.text: If replicas do not respond within a timeout, coordinator retries or fails gracefully.

blocks.html: Leader/Primary node
All writes go through a single leader to reduce conflicts and simplify ordering.
blocks.text: All writes go through a single leader to reduce conflicts and simplify ordering.

blocks.html: Ensures linearizability (strict consistency).
Write batching
Combine multiple write requests into a single batch to reduce network round trips.
blocks.text: Combine multiple write requests into a single batch to reduce network round trips.
